opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's the question I think about more than almost anything else. A lot of science-driven companies have a moment where the technology is real and exciting, but it hasn't yet found the place in the world where it actually pays for itself. For olfaction, I've tried to be really honest about that from the beginning.

The way I frame it is that digitizing smell is a long journey, and you can't fund a twenty-year journey purely on promises. You need a near-term reason to exist that creates real value for real customers, and ideally that same activity pushes the core science forward. So the question becomes: where does smell already matter economically today?

The answer is fragrance. It's a large, mature industry. Scent is in your shampoo, your laundry detergent, your candles, your fine perfume. That industry runs on the same thing we're trying to master, which is understanding the relationship between molecules and what people perceive. Historically it has been driven by intuition and a lot of trial and error, and it's had real constraints. Ingredients get regulated away, supply chains for natural materials are fragile, and there's demand for molecules that are safer, more sustainable, or perform better. If you can predict what a molecule will smell like before you make it, you can explore chemical space far more efficiently than someone who has to synthesize and sniff thousands of candidates.

So there's a good fit between what our models are good at and what this industry needs. And the virtuous cycle is the important part. Every time we design, make, and evaluate new molecules and formulations, we generate high-quality perceptual data, and that's the scarcest resource in this whole field. Vision had ImageNet and audio had huge recorded corpora. Smell had nothing comparable. Doing commercial work is how we build that dataset in a way that's sustainable, instead of relying on grant cycles.

The second piece is being disciplined about sequencing. There are moonshot applications people get excited about, like detecting disease from scent, or sending a smell the way you send a photo. I believe in those, but they need more fundamental capabilities: better sensors, a better map of odor space, a way to read and write scent reliably. If you try to jump straight there, you burn out before you arrive. So you take on problems that are valuable now, that fund the work, and that build the capabilities you need for the next, harder problem.

And culturally, you need a team that holds both of those things at once. People who care deeply about the scientific mission, and people who understand that a customer has to want what you're making. Getting those two groups to respect each other, and seeing commercial work as part of the mission rather than a distraction, is a big part of making it self-sustaining.

r001.rationale: The response calls detecting disease from scent a moonshot that depends on more fundamental capabilities, but it does not identify medical diagnostics as a commercially difficult market.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about constantly, because the science is only half the problem. When I was at Google Brain, we showed you could predict what a molecule smells like from its structure, and that was a genuine breakthrough. But a breakthrough is not a business. Nobody wakes up in the morning saying, "I wish I had an olfactory map today."

So the way I frame it is: digitizing smell is the mission, and the mission is decades long. But a company has to eat along the way. You can't just burn capital for twenty years hoping the market shows up. You have to find places where the technology, as it exists right now, solves a problem someone already has budget for.

For us, the first obvious one is fragrance and flavor. That's a huge industry, something like tens of billions of dollars, and the core workflow is still very artisanal. A perfumer or a flavorist is sitting there with a palette of a few thousand ingredients, iterating by hand. If you can hand them a model that says, "here's a molecule that smells like sandalwood, is sustainable, is biodegradable, and nobody's ever made before," that's immediately valuable. We've actually done that. We've designed new molecules, had them synthesized, had trained panels smell them, and the predictions hold up. So that's revenue that exists today, not revenue we're hoping exists in 2035.

The second piece is the other direction, which is reading the world rather than designing for it. Sensors. Can you detect disease on breath, spoilage in food, a leak in a factory? That's the part that's technically harder and takes longer, but it's also where the market gets enormous. The analogy I keep coming back to is the camera. Nobody in the 1990s was sitting around going "I need a camera on my phone." But once vision got cheap and digital, it became infrastructure. I think smell has that same shape. It's just earlier.

And honestly, the discipline this forces on you is healthy. If you have to sell something, you have to be right about what the technology can actually do, not what you wish it could do. Every customer conversation is a form of peer review that's much more brutal than any conference. So I don't see the commercial side as a distraction from the science. It's the thing that keeps the science honest and keeps the lights on long enough to finish the map.

r001.rationale: The response says disease detection on breath is technically harder and takes longer, but does not identify medical diagnostics as a commercially difficult market.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to find a place where solving a real customer problem also helps you build the underlying technology. You can have a very ambitious vision for digitizing smell, but a vision isn’t a business model. You need to ask: Who needs this today? What decision can they make better with it? And is that improvement valuable enough that they’ll pay for it?

Fragrance is a natural place to start, because smell is already the product. If you can help someone find a molecule with the scent they want, while also meeting constraints around cost and performance, there’s a concrete reason to use your technology.

The challenge is making those individual applications reinforce a broader capability. Ideally, the work you do for customers generates learning that makes the next problem easier to solve. Revenue supports the science, and the science makes the product more useful. That’s the loop I’d want to build—a business that can sustain progress toward the bigger vision.

r001.rationale: The response discusses fragrance as a starting market and the general challenge of building a business, but does not identify medical diagnostics as commercially difficult.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to connect the science to a problem that somebody already needs solved. Building a machine that can smell is an exciting technical goal, but it isn’t, by itself, a business. You have to ask: Who needs to understand or create a smell, what do they do today, and how could we make that process better?

Fragrance is a natural place to start, because smell is the product. If we can help people discover useful molecules or develop a fragrance more efficiently, there’s a clear reason for someone to pay for that capability. And that revenue can support the research needed to make the technology more general.

That’s how I think about making it self-sustaining: find a valuable application where the technology works today, deliver something people will pay for, and use what you learn to expand what’s possible. You can have a very ambitious vision for digitizing smell while being very concrete about the first customer problem you solve.

r001.rationale: The response discusses fragrance as a starting market and does not identify medical diagnostics or describe it as commercially difficult.
